newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: IMF warns Slovak economy in danger of overheating.
newsitem.headline: IMF warns Slovak economy in danger of overheating.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has warned Slovakia its economy was in danger of overheating and urged the introduction of stricter financial policies to curb domestic consumption.

In a report made public on Wednesday, the IMF said signs of an overheating economy could be seen in the significant deterioration of the current account which ran a $1.5 billion deficit in 1996 after a $648.8 million surplus in 1995.
"After three years of fast economic growth and decreasing inflation the Slovak economy shows signs of overheating," the report, resulting from an IMF mission to Slovakia in October, said.
"A further signal of overheating is the fast growth of real wages which increased by 12 percent over the past 12 months and to a high degree surpassed the growth of productivity," it added.

The report said that over 20 percent growth in domestic consumption also contributed to the worsening of the current account, which in 1996 was some 10 percentage points of GDP higher than in the previous year.
"Such a level of the current account deficit is untenable as, with regard to the low level of direct foreign investment, would lead to high growth of foreign debt," the IMF said.
The report said that for this reason, the IMF recommends a "stricter financial policy aimed at reducing domestic consumption".
It said the key to Slovakia's economic policy was to find the optimum method of a return to a sustainable development of the current account.
"Apart from tightening financial policy, the worsening of export competitiveness, a result of the fast growth of real wages in the past two years, must also be stopped," it said.

The report said the IMF projected Slovakia's 1997 GDP growth at five percent with an average inflation of five percent. At the end of 1996, inflation stood at 5.4 percent, while GDP growth of 6.8-7.0 percent is expected.

"It is assumed that under present conditions the fiscal deficit will increase to some 19 billion crowns ($580 million), which is 2.9 percent of the GDP, with the state budget deficit at around five billion crowns and the deficit of non-budgetary projects should total 16 billion crowns," the report said. ($1=32.54 Slovak Crown)
